lesson.title: Constructor: Building an Object in One Line
lesson.summary: A constructor is the overall process of creating a new object and getting it ready to use; in Python that process is triggered by calling ClassName(...), which builds the object and then hands it to __init__ to be set up.
lesson.body:
You've now seen that writing Dog("Fido", 3) creates a fully set-up Dog object in a single line, with __init__ automatically filling in its attributes. That whole act, creating an object and getting it into a valid starting state, is what programmers mean by "the constructor." It's worth pausing on this because the term describes a process, and __init__ is the piece of that process you actually write.

In many languages, the constructor and the initializer are one and the same thing you write yourself. Python actually splits object creation into two steps behind the scenes. A method called __new__ is responsible for actually building the raw object in memory, and only after that succeeds does Python call __init__ on the freshly built object to configure it. You will almost never write __new__ yourself in ordinary code; Python's default version handles it perfectly well. But knowing it exists explains something that otherwise seems arbitrary: __init__ never needs to return the object, because the object already exists by the time __init__ runs. Its only job is to initialize, not to build from nothing.

For everyday purposes, though, you can think of calling Dog("Fido", 3) as "calling the constructor," and __init__ as the code that constructor runs to set the object up. Here's the key behavior that makes constructors worth caring about: every call creates a completely independent object, even if the arguments look similar.

```python
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

rex = Dog("Rex", 5)
bella = Dog("Bella", 2)

print(rex.name, rex.age)
# Output: Rex 5
print(bella.name, bella.age)
# Output: Bella 2
print(rex is bella)
# Output: False
```

Each call to Dog(...) runs the full construction process from scratch: a new object is built, __init__ runs with self bound to that new object, and the attributes are filled in from whatever arguments were passed that time. rex and bella end up with different values stored in their own separate name and age attributes, which is why print(rex.name, rex.age) shows Rex 5 while print(bella.name, bella.age) shows Bella 2. The last line, rex is bella, checks whether the two variables point to the exact same object in memory, and since two separate construction calls produced two separate objects, the answer is False, even though both objects came from the identical class and the identical constructor code.
